clinicalPearls: Characterised by severe intellectual disability, near-absent speech, and a happy demeanour with frequent laughter and smiling
Movement disorder features ataxia, jerky limb movements, and a characteristic wide-based, stiff gait
A history of frequent bursts of laughter, hand-flapping, and excitable behaviour is a helpful clinical clue
Seizures usually begin in early childhood and are often accompanied by a distinctive EEG pattern even between clinical seizures
Microcephaly, a wide mouth with widely spaced teeth, and a prominent chin become more apparent with age
Caused by loss of function of the maternally inherited UBE3A gene at 15q11-q13, most commonly a maternal deletion
Represents the reciprocal imprinting disorder to Prader-Willi syndrome at the same chromosomal locus
Sleep disturbance with reduced sleep need is common and can be very disruptive for families
reference.pathophysiology: Angelman syndrome is caused by loss of function of the maternally expressed UBE3A gene within the imprinted 15q11-q13 region. In neurons, only the maternal UBE3A copy is active because the paternal copy is silenced, so loss of the maternal allele leaves neurons without functional UBE3A, which encodes a ubiquitin ligase important for synaptic regulation. The most common mechanism is a de novo maternal deletion; other causes include paternal uniparental disomy, an imprinting defect, and UBE3A point mutations. The resulting neuronal dysfunction produces the severe developmental impairment, movement disorder, and epilepsy.
additionalInvestigations: DNA methylation analysis of 15q11-q13 as the initial diagnostic test
Follow-up studies to define mechanism, including UBE3A sequencing when methylation is normal but suspicion persists
Electroencephalography, which often shows a characteristic pattern
Sleep assessment when disturbance is significant
redFlags: Frequent or prolonged seizures, including status epilepticus, requiring prompt management
Feeding and swallowing difficulties with aspiration risk in infancy
Scoliosis developing with age needing orthopaedic surveillance
Severe communication impairment necessitating augmentative communication support
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is near normal, but severe intellectual disability and lack of speech persist lifelong; seizures often improve after childhood, and quality of life depends on multidisciplinary support and communication aids.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing as cerebral palsy and missing the genetic cause
Assuming a normal methylation test excludes the diagnosis when UBE3A mutation testing is still needed
Overlooking the marked and treatable sleep disturbance
management: Anticonvulsant therapy for the epilepsy, favouring agents such as valproate, levetiracetam and benzodiazepines while avoiding drugs that may aggravate the seizures
Communication intervention with augmentative and alternative communication systems given the near-absent speech
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy for ataxia, gait and motor function, with orthotics where needed
Management of sleep disturbance through sleep-hygiene measures and melatonin
Behavioural strategies and support for hyperactivity and feeding, with surveillance for scoliosis and gastro-oesophageal reflux
Coordinated multidisciplinary neurodevelopmental follow-up with family and carer support
Genetic counselling with recurrence-risk assessment tailored to the underlying mechanism, whether maternal deletion, uniparental disomy, imprinting defect or UBE3A mutation
